blocks.x: The signals
Three data points from September and October 2026 matter to Winnipeg landlords thinking about longer holds and longer tenancies:

**Sales slowed.** The [Winnipeg Regional Real Estate Board](https://www.winnipegregionalrealestatenews.com/market-statistics/market-releases/article/629/more-choice-record-average-prices-and-softer-sales-defined-september-results) reported September sales down about 10% year over year, level with the five-year average, with listings up about 14%.

**Borrowing costs rose.** The Bank of Canada [raised its policy rate to 2.50%](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/10/fad-press-release-2026-10-28/) on October 28, 2026, which can make borrowing to buy or refinance more expensive.

**Rents flattened.** [liv.rent's October 2026 Winnipeg rent report](https://liv.rent/blog/?p=69631) showed the average unfurnished one-bedroom asking rent at $1,319, with three straight monthly declines since the July peak of $1,353, though it was still up 1.7% from a year earlier.

Put together, investors who might have sold in 2027 may have reasons to wait. None of these numbers measures how long tenants stay, and [CMHC's 2025 rental report](https://eppd1strscr01.blob.core.windows.net/cmhcprdcontainer/sf/project/archive/housing_markets/rentalmarketreportcanadaandselectedmarkets/rental-market-report-2025-fall-en.pdf) says more vacant options drove turnover in Winnipeg. So a longer tenancy is not something the market will hand you. It is something to plan and renovate for.
Why longer tenancies change a landlord's renovation strategy

The traditional unit-turn model assumes a tenant leaves every year or two and the landlord refreshes the unit in between. That model rewards cheap, fast cosmetics: a coat of paint, a deep clean, maybe a new faucet.

Longer tenancies flip the logic. If a good tenant stays four or five years, the landlord's biggest risk is not a slow turn. It is losing that tenant to a newer building because the unit, the hallway or the windows feel worn.
And when that tenant does eventually leave, the unit needs more than a coat of paint, because five years of wear has accumulated.
That shifts the value toward property renovation services that last:
**Durable flooring** (luxury vinyl plank or similar) that survives years of wear rather than carpet that needs replacing every turn.
**Quality paint systems** in scrubbable finishes, especially in hallways and common areas.
**Windows and doors** that cut drafts and noise, which tenants notice every day in a Winnipeg winter.
**Masonry and envelope repairs** that help prevent the water damage that makes units unrentable.
Our view: renovate for the tenant you want to keep

Longer holds are an opportunity to change how landlords think about capital spending. Instead of asking "what is the cheapest way to get this unit rented," the better question is "what would make my best tenant stay another three years?"

That question leads to different priorities. Common areas matter more, because every tenant uses them every day. Comfort matters more: a drafty window or a door that will not latch is a daily reminder that the building is not cared for.
And timing matters: upgrades made while the tenant is still there build loyalty, while upgrades made only between tenants are invisible to the people who would have stayed.
The rent-rule backdrop

Manitoba's rent guideline for 2027 is 3%, and the province announced it was [expanding rent regulation](https://news.gov.mb.ca/news/?archive=&item=75138) by raising the exemption threshold from $1,670 to $2,000 per month on January 1, 2027. That brings more units under the guideline. Landlords who want to recover part of their capital costs may need to apply for an [above-guideline increase](https://www.gov.mb.ca/cca/rtb/landlord/aboveguide.html) through the Residential Tenancies Branch.

[On October 30, 2026](https://web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/regs/annual/2026/116.php), Manitoba reduced by 40% how much of a capital cost counts in an above-guideline application. Depending on the item, 20%, 15%, 10% or 7.5% of the cost counts from that date. Also, as of October 20, 2026, a tenant pays nothing toward a proposed above-guideline increase until the Branch rules.

Only costs already paid or billed can be claimed, and rebates have to be listed. That makes good records and clear scopes from contractors more valuable. Itemized invoices, before-and-after photos and clear descriptions of work help support any application.
A longer-hold renovation plan
**Audit your building like a tenant would.** Walk the entrance, hallways, laundry and a typical unit. Note what feels dated or uncomfortable.
**Fix the envelope first.** [Windows, doors](/services/windows-and-doors) and [masonry](/services/masonry-stucco) protect everything inside.
**Upgrade common areas next.** Paint, flooring and lighting in shared spaces affect every resident.
**Plan unit upgrades by durability.** Choose finishes that will last through a five-year tenancy.
**Document everything** in case you pursue an above-guideline increase.

Check for asbestos before old materials are disturbed. The Province says it was used in buildings built or renovated before 1990, and our guide covers [asbestos testing before you renovate](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba).
What to watch in the next six months

Three signals will tell landlords whether the longer-hold thesis is playing out. First, the Bank of Canada's rate decisions in 2027: another increase could further slow resale activity and make holding even more attractive than selling.

Second, the Winnipeg Regional Real Estate Board's monthly listing counts. If listings grow faster than sales through winter, spring sellers will face more competition and more investors may choose to wait.
Third, renewal rates in your own portfolio. If more tenants are renewing than a year ago, that is the clearest sign tenancies are lengthening.
The bottom line

Longer holds reward durable decisions. A cheap fix that has to be redone at every turn made sense when units turned over every year and resale was the exit plan. When you plan to hold longer and want good tenants to stay, the better investment is work that lasts, from the envelope inward.
